messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina is a 30-year-old school counselor who had been proud of being the calm adult in the room, the person students sought out when they were frightened or overwhelmed. That sense of herself changed after an encounter with police nine months ago. She and her husband had been driving home from a friend’s birthday party when they were pulled over late at night. The officer approached the car already tense. Amina remembers the sharp smell of alcohol on his breath when he leaned toward her window, though she had not been drinking, and the crackle of his radio mixed with his raised voice. When her husband turned suddenly to reach for the registration in the glove compartment, the officer shouted and grabbed for his weapon. Amina froze. She can still recall how quickly ordinary movement became dangerous, how the officer’s abrupt gestures and yelling made the whole scene feel one second away from catastrophe. She believes she spoke at the wrong moment and moved too quickly when asked for her ID. Even now, what stays with her is the conviction that if she had acted differently, the stop would not have escalated the way it did.

In the weeks afterward, Amina tried to carry on at work, sitting with students in her office and walking noisy hallways between classes, but she no longer felt like the same person. She had come to believe there was something wrong with her, that other people could absorb a frightening experience and move on whereas she had somehow been ruined by it. She felt set apart even from her husband, who wanted to reassure her that they had survived and were safe. Because she blamed herself for how she had responded during the stop, she began shrinking away from anything that stirred strong feeling. If she sensed herself getting upset, she would abruptly change the subject, leave the room, or tell people she was tired. Invitations from friends were declined, not only because she did not want to talk about what happened, but because even the possibility of feeling happy or hopeful seemed risky, as if letting her guard down would expose how damaged she really was. She increasingly kept to herself, both at home and at school.

That withdrawal gradually altered the shape of her days. At work, she started eating lunch alone in her office with the door closed rather than in the staff room. She limited casual conversations with teachers and kept student meetings tightly structured so nothing emotional would spill beyond what she felt able to manage. After school, she often went straight home and avoided social visits entirely. Living that way made her world smaller and lonelier, and the loneliness fed what she already believed about herself: that she was no longer like other people, that she had become isolated in some fundamental way. The more she avoided situations that might bring warmth, closeness, or strong feeling, the more convincing it seemed that there really was something broken in her.

Her beliefs also kept her body in a state of readiness. Because she saw herself as someone who had failed in a dangerous moment, she was certain she could not trust herself to judge safety properly again. That conviction made her intensely watchful. In the school hallways, sudden movements by students—an arm thrown up in excitement, a teenager rushing past her doorway—put her immediately on guard. She scans entrances, notices who is moving quickly, and sits in meetings where she can see the door. Even at home on the couch beside her husband, she finds she cannot relax, though part of her knows she is in a safe place. When she catches herself monitoring everyone around her like this, it seems to confirm her harshest view of herself: normal people do not live braced for impact, she thinks, so there must be something deeply wrong with her.

That constant alarm has, in turn, made the world feel full of reminders. On days when she is exhausted, her control slips and she becomes especially vulnerable to being pulled back into the stop. Loud noises in the school building—the slam of a locker, a shouted voice in the corridor, the sudden burst of the PA system—make her heart jump before she can think. If she passes a parent at pickup who smells of alcohol, she feels a jolt of dread and has to fight the urge to leave. Because she has narrowed her life so much, she arrives at work already depleted, and in that worn-down state the triggers feel even closer to the surface. To protect herself she avoids assemblies, noisy common areas, celebratory staff events, and difficult conversations with colleagues or family; yet this constant retreat leaves her even more tense and watchful, as if danger is always just about to break through.

By the time Amina sought help, her husband had begun telling her that he missed her even when she was sitting next to him. At school, she was worried students were noticing how easily she startled and how often she cut meetings short. What finally brought her in was not one dramatic setback but the realization that she was living every day as though that traffic stop were still unfolding. She is frightened that if she keeps going this way, she will end up entirely cut off from other people and unable to do the work that once mattered most to her. At the same time, she is quietly hoping that treatment might help her feel less on guard, less ashamed, and less alone.
